messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Nabil was 56, a Middle Eastern American man who had lived in the United States for most of his adult life, married for more than three decades, and working in social media management, a job that kept him in front of screens for much of the day. The police violence that he described as the turning point in his life happened in a moment that should have been ordinary: he had been out in public, approached by officers, and then found himself pinned, shouted at, and unable to make himself understood quickly enough. What remained most sharply in his mind was not a neat sequence but fragments that came back with the force of the body. He could still taste what he had tasted during the event when the memory returned, as if the same stale, metallic taste rose in his mouth whenever his mind brushed against it. He did not let himself stay with the memory for long; even now, he would push it away before he could fully recall it, cutting off the scene as soon as it started to form, because once it opened up he felt a surge of intense rage that was hard for him to settle.

In the weeks and months afterward, Nabil became someone who was always orienting himself to danger. He constantly scanned his surroundings for signs of threat, not in a dramatic way but in a practiced, exhausting way that had become automatic when he walked into a store, entered a parking lot, or sat in a waiting room. He always identified escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere, noting exits, corners, and places where he could get out quickly if he needed to. Even in places that other people would have thought safe, he was unable to relax. He described sitting at family gatherings with his shoulders tight, his attention never fully on the conversation, because the feeling of safety did not settle in his body. What frightened him most was the strength of the emotions that followed him now: fear, horror, anger, and shame would come up with little warning, and he often felt overwhelmed by the fact that they were still so close to the surface. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, not in an abstract philosophical sense but in the concrete sense that a normal day could turn quickly and without warning. Alongside that, he had lost trust in other people. People were not what they seemed, he felt; authority, friendliness, or calm words could change in an instant, and he no longer assumed that someone approaching him meant well.

Nabil also noticed that the event had altered how he saw himself. He thought often that he had acted in ways that went against who he was, though he struggled to say this without sounding disloyal to himself. He had once seen himself as measured, respectful, and able to handle pressure, but in the memory he felt there had been moments when he was not himself, when fear and humiliation had made him react in ways he still judged harshly. That appraisal sat heavily with him, especially because he could not yet bring the memory into full focus without stopping it short. He was left with pieces rather than a complete account, and the pieces were enough to make him feel both angry and contaminated by what had happened.

Over time his avoidance spread beyond the original event. He avoided anything that could bring up negative or even positive feelings, because he did not want to be thrown back into the emotional intensity that followed the memory. He also avoided media about similar events, turning away from television programmes, films, or articles that showed police violence, protests, or confrontations that resembled what had happened to him. In his work as a social media manager, this could be especially difficult because his role required him to look through a stream of content all day. He found himself closing tabs, skipping clips, and asking colleagues to take over when posts or videos began to resemble the kind of incident that he could not bear to watch. That avoidance had made parts of his job harder and less satisfying, and his wife had noticed that he was less present at home too, more likely to sit in silence or leave the room when family discussion turned emotional.

By the time he sought help, Nabil was worn down by the combination of constant alertness, the effort of keeping memories at bay, and the conviction that he could no longer assume the world or other people were safe. He came to treatment because he was tired of living as if every place required an exit plan and every unfamiliar face might conceal danger. What he hoped for was not to forget what had happened, but to be able to think about it without being flooded by rage and fear, and to sit in a room, with his wife or at work, without always feeling that he needed to be ready to run.
